faq.q: How does light stay inside a fibre?
faq.a: The core is surrounded by cladding glass in which light travels slightly faster. When light hits that boundary at a shallow angle it cannot escape and reflects back completely. This is total internal reflection, and it guides the light along even round gentle bends.
The cladding is a layer of slightly different glass around the core. Because light travels a little faster in it, the boundary acts like a perfect mirror and keeps the light in the core.
asks: Why does an optical fibre have two layers of glass?

faq.q: Why is fibre faster than copper broadband?
faq.a: Light in very pure glass fades far less than electrical signals in copper and is not disturbed by electrical noise, so fibre can carry much more data much further without boosting.
Yes, gently. Strength fibres and a jacket protect the glass, but a very tight bend lets light leak out of the core or can crack the glass, so installers follow a minimum bend radius.
asks: Is the glass in a fibre cable fragile?

faq.q: How much data can one fibre carry?
faq.a: By sending many colours of laser light down the same fibre at once, each carrying its own data, a single strand can carry many terabits per second, enough for millions of video calls.
asks: How fast can optical fibre go?

facts: Light in glass fibre travels at about two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum, roughly 200,000 kilometres per second.
Charles Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for showing how glass fibres could carry light over long distances.

quiz.why: Light meeting the core-cladding boundary at a shallow angle is reflected back completely.
